title: Making the case for a rewrite, then building the plugin framework
question: Tell me about a time you convinced someone to invest in technical work.

situation: The legacy desktop client had evolved into a tightly coupled monolith. Different modules had been developed independently over time, so they were not always consistent in how they worked and often had noticeably different UI patterns.

The lack of consistency was also reflected in the code: similar concepts and behaviours were implemented differently across modules, making the system harder to understand and increasing the effort required to add or change functionality.
Adding a new feature often meant changing existing code in several places, making development slower and increasing the risk of regressions.
task: I believed that continuing to add features on top of the existing architecture would become increasingly expensive, so I needed to convince management to invest in a partial rewrite rather than spending the entire development effort on the next immediate feature.

I also needed to turn that investment into something practical: a plugin framework that could decouple new modules from the core desktop engine while providing a more consistent foundation for both their implementation and user experience, without requiring us to rewrite the entire application.
action: I built the case around the business impact rather than presenting it as a purely technical preference. I showed how the existing coupling and inconsistent module implementations were increasing the cost and risk of feature development, and explained how investing in the core architecture would make subsequent features faster and safer to deliver.

Once I had buy-in, I designed and implemented a dynamic plugin framework in C# using reflection. Individual modules could be developed and loaded independently, allowing new functionality to be integrated without modifying or recompiling unrelated modules.

The framework also established common infrastructure for the modules, so developers no longer had to repeatedly solve the same integration and UI problems in different ways. I used this to improve the consistency of the dynamic UI, including real-time validation feedback directly within the UI tables so invalid data could be identified before submission.
Throughout the migration, I had to preserve complex legacy business behaviour, so I worked incrementally rather than attempting to replace the entire client in one step.
result: The new architecture significantly reduced the effort required to develop and integrate subsequent features, while making the existing desktop application more stable and easier to extend.

One of the first new modules built on the framework was relatively small, but could be created and integrated in less than two hours because most of the surrounding infrastructure was handled automatically.
The investment established a reusable architectural foundation rather than solving the problem for just one feature, while also giving future modules a more consistent technical and UI foundation.

challenge: The hardest part was changing the architecture without breaking the behaviour that customers already relied on. The legacy application contained a large amount of business logic whose interactions were not always obvious, and different modules had evolved with their own implementations and assumptions. Every piece moved into the new architecture therefore had to preserve those behaviours while becoming more isolated and consistent.
hardestBug: I ran into difficult state inconsistencies in dynamic Windows Forms tables where the UI event lifecycle behaved differently from the sequence I expected. Standard event handlers were firing in unexpected combinations during dynamic layout changes, so I had to trace the lower-level rendering and event flow to understand where the state was becoming inconsistent.
differently: I would establish automated behavioural regression tests before starting the migration. At the time, validating that the refactored implementation preserved the legacy behaviour required significant manual testing. A suite comparing the old and new behaviour would have caught regressions earlier and made the migration much safer to iterate on.
aboutYourself: The project showed me that I enjoy solving foundational problems that make other engineers more effective. I found it particularly rewarding to take a chaotic, tightly coupled system with inconsistent implementations and create architectural boundaries that made future development simpler.
enjoyed: Seeing the individual modules become dramatically simpler once the framework was in place. Features that previously required changes across the monolith could become self-contained plugins, while the shared framework handled much of the integration work automatically. Seeing a new module go from idea to integrated functionality in less than two hours made the architectural improvement very tangible.
